passage:
Sit, Irfan, and listen. It's your Dada Akash speaking. When I was ten, the current went off every afternoon from noon, and my mother said, "Go and play." I whined that there was nothing to do. For an hour I did nothing at all.
Then I looked at the yard. A broken cot, some old saris on the line, a bucket. By evening I had built a fort with a flag. The next day my friends came, and we invented a game with mango stones and a chalk line. Nobody told me what to do.
I think that boredom was like a field before the crop. It looked empty, and something started to grow.

qa.q: What did Akash build in the yard?
qa.a: A fort with a flag, from a broken cot, old saris and a bucket.

qa.q: How did Akash feel during that first hour of nothing?
qa.a: Restless and complaining. Akash whined that there was nothing to do.

qa.q: What choice did young Akash make that turned the boredom around?
qa.a: After an hour of doing nothing Akash looked at what lay around the yard and began building, without anyone telling Akash what to do.

qa.q: What might Akash's friends have found the next day if Akash had not built the fort?
qa.a: Probably nothing to play with, since the fort and the game began because Akash used the empty afternoon.

grounding: A child without screens on a long afternoon builds a fort and a game, so tolerated boredom becomes invention.

passage:
Rain hammered the windows, the internet had gone, and Papa was on a work call in the next room. "No screens, Jasleen," whispered her father Francis through the door. "I need quiet."
Jasleen sighed at the ceiling. Then she dragged two bedsheets over the clothes-drying rack and the dining chairs, slid in with a torch, and drew a map of a country called Puddle.
By the time the call ended, the fort had a door, a flag, a rule book, and a toll of one biscuit. Francis crawled in, paid up, and was told to sit properly.

qa.q: What was the toll to enter Jasleen's fort?
qa.a: One biscuit.

qa.q: What does Jasleen feel when she sighs at the ceiling, and how does that change?
qa.a: She is annoyed and bored at first, then becomes absorbed and pleased with her fort and its rules.

qa.q: What could Francis do next time there is no screen and he needs quiet?
qa.a: He could leave out bedsheets, chairs and paper and let Jasleen invent something, as she did, and tell her when his call will end.

qa.q: How might Francis feel crawling into the fort after his call?
qa.a: Probably pleased and surprised, since he pays the toll and accepts being bossed around. 😊

grounding: A child left without screens on a rainy afternoon builds a fort and a game.

passage:
At the community centre's summer camp, the tablets were locked away after lunch because of a power cut. Ojas slumped on a bench. "This is the worst camp ever." Yamini, on the next bench, was just as bored.
For twenty minutes they did nothing but complain and swing their legs.
Then Ojas noticed the stack of old cardboard boxes by the storeroom. "What if we made a tunnel?" They dragged the boxes into the hall, taped them end to end, and cut windows with safety scissors. By four o'clock the tunnel went all the way round the ping-pong table, with a ticket counter and a secret exit.
When the power came back, the camp teacher announced the tablets were free. Ojas didn't even look up. "We're adding a second floor."

qa.q: Where did the tunnel go?
qa.a: All the way round the ping-pong table.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel before noticing the boxes?
qa.a: Ojas felt bored and grumpy, calling it the worst camp ever.

qa.q: What helped the tunnel idea arrive?
qa.a: Twenty minutes of boredom without screens, plus boxes lying around, gave Ojas room to invent something.

qa.q: How might the camp teacher see Ojas ignoring the tablets?
qa.a: The camp teacher might be surprised and pleased that the children chose their own tunnel over the screens.

grounding: Shows children without screens on a long afternoon turning boredom into building a tunnel.

passage:
Monday. At Vinita Nani's house for the holidays there was no TV and no tablet. Parul lay on the charpai all afternoon. "Nani, there's NOTHING here." Nani just kept shelling peas.
Wednesday. Parul found an old notebook and a pencil in Nani's cupboard. She drew the goat next door. Then the goat wearing sunglasses. Then the goat as a king, with a tiny crown.
Saturday. The notebook was full: a whole comic called "Goat King of Lucknow", with speech bubbles and a map of the kingdom. Parul made Nani read it twice, then started volume two.

qa.q: What was Parul's comic called?
qa.a: "Goat King of Lucknow".

qa.q: How did Parul feel on Monday?
qa.a: Parul felt bored and fed up, lying on the charpai complaining that there was nothing to do.

qa.q: What did Nani do that helped the comic happen?
qa.a: Nani didn't rush to entertain her; she kept shelling peas and let the boredom run its course.

qa.q: How might Vinita Nani feel reading the comic twice?
qa.a: Nani likely felt proud and amused to see the neighbour's goat turned into a king.

grounding: Shows a child left without screens in the holidays whose boredom turns into days of drawing a comic.

passage:
Vishal, you say you're bored without your tablet? Sit. When I was ten, in our Nagpur chawl, summer holidays meant forty days of heat and nothing. No TV in our house. The first week I sulked on the steps and counted crows.
Then one afternoon I started collecting bottle caps from the tea stall. By evening I had twenty-two. I drew a football pitch in chalk on the corridor floor and flicked the caps like players. My friend Sunil joined. Then his sister. By the end of that summer half the chawl had teams, a league table on the wall and a trophy made from a tin cup.
I, your Akash Dada, never had a better summer. And it all started with those days of counting crows.

qa.q: How many bottle caps did Akash collect by the first evening?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: How did Akash feel in the first week of the holidays?
qa.a: Akash felt bored and sulky, sitting on the steps counting crows.

qa.q: Which choice turned Akash's boredom around?
qa.a: Collecting bottle caps and drawing a chalk pitch to flick them like players, which grew into a whole league.

qa.q: How did Sunil and the others take to the game?
qa.a: They joined eagerly: Sunil, then his sister, then half the chawl, with teams, a league table and a trophy.

grounding: Shows a child with no screens on long summer days whose boredom turns into inventing a game.

passage:
The power went off at noon in their Jaipur colony and didn't come back all afternoon. No fan, no television, no charging the tablet. Siddharth, ten, lay on the floor and moaned, "There's NOTHING to do."
His sister Bhavna, fourteen, was reading. "Then do nothing."
He did nothing for twenty minutes. It was awful. Then he looked at the bedsheets, the dining chairs, and the broom.
By three o'clock there was a fort in the living room, with a sheet roof and a flag made from a pencil and a sock. By four, he had invented a game called "Fort Defence" with rules written on a notebook page, and Bhavna had joined as the attacking army.
When the power came back at six, the TV blinked on. Siddharth didn't look. "Wait, we haven't finished the siege."

qa.q: What did Siddharth use for the fort's flag?
qa.a: The flag was made from a pencil and a sock.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel during the twenty minutes of doing nothing?
qa.a: Siddharth felt bored and restless, finding the empty time awful before ideas began to come.

qa.q: Why did the power cut turn out well for Siddharth?
qa.a: Without screens, he had to sit through boredom, and that is where the fort and his own game grew.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have seen her brother's fort by the end?
qa.a: Bhavna likely found it fun and impressive enough to join in as the attacking army.

grounding: Left without screens on a long afternoon, a child moves through boredom to build a fort and invent a game.
